text:
In a synthetic organic lab, chemists commonly check reaction progress and purity by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) or monitor preparative column chromatography. When two different compounds have nearly the same polarity, they travel up the TLC plate (or through the column) at essentially the same rate. The spots or bands then appear literally “on top of each other,” making separation difficult. That is the idiomatic way many chemists describe co-eluting compounds.

• Similar boiling points (A) would affect a distillation, but chemists usually say the “b.p.’s are too close,” rather than “on top of each other.”  
• Similar optical rotations (B) is not something one would phrase this way.  
• Non-covalent interactions between the molecules (C) would not be described as being “on top of each other” in everyday lab talk.  
• Similar polarity (D) directly leads to overlapping spots/bands in TLC or column work, matching the expression used.

Therefore the best interpretation is:

Answer: D
